Build a heatmap in the browser

Source: R/heat_map_app.R
heat_map_app.Rd

heat_map_app() opens an app in a web browser (or the RStudio or Positron viewer) to build a heatmap without writing code: drop a table or a single-cell file on its start page (or start from data in R or an example), choose what each column does - cells of the heatmap, groups or annotations of the rows - and set any of the arguments of heat_map while the heatmap is drawn again: scaling, clustering and dendrograms, colours, cells and their text, labels, legends, tracks and bars, marks and zooms. Hovering over the heatmap shows the values of its cells, and rows and columns selected on it (by clicking or dragging) can be shown alone, labelled or copied. Each change can be undone, the R code that draws the heatmap again is written beside it, and the heatmap downloads as a PNG, PDF, SVG, TIFF or JPEG image of a chosen size.

Usage

heat_map_app(
  x = NULL,
  ...,
  allow_code = TRUE,
  max_upload = 1024,
  launch.browser = interactive()
)

Arguments

x

data to start with: a matrix, data frame or single-cell object (anything heat_map() draws), or the name of a file to read (as above). Set to NULL by default to start on a page to drop a file or choose an example (tables and single-cell data).

...

settings to start with, named by the arguments of heat_map, e.g. scale = "column".

allow_code

logical indicating whether settings may be R code run in this R session (such as rainbow(5) or x$mpg), set to TRUE by default. Set it to FALSE before hosting the app for other people: settings are then limited to numbers, text, TRUE, FALSE, NA, NULL and c() or list() of them.

max_upload

the size of the largest file that can be uploaded, in megabytes, set to 1024 by default.

launch.browser

whether the app opens in a browser when it runs, as in runApp: TRUE in interactive sessions by default.

Value

a Shiny app (from shinyApp), which runs when it is printed (as at the console) or given to shiny::runApp(). The app needs the shiny and bslib packages.

Details

Files can be CSV, TSV or other delimited text (.csv, .tsv, .tab or .txt), Excel files (.xlsx or .xls, read with the readxl package), R data (.rds: a matrix, data frame or single-cell object) or AnnData files (.h5ad, read with heat_map_read_h5ad). The first column of a table is used as its row names when it holds unique text. Tables show their columns (one row per row of the table), and their columns can also group the rows (group_by) or annotate them (annotation_by); single-cell data show the chosen features, grouped and annotated by the cells' metadata. Heatmaps can also be dot plots of groups (heat_map_dot) or correlations between the columns (heat_map_cor).

Every argument of heat_map() has a setting, in sections down the side of the page (the most used with plain labels and inputs made for them, the rest under "More settings"), with the argument's name and its documentation, and a search box finds them. Settings left at their defaults are left out of the code. Settings that take R values that belong to the data (e.g. bar_values_y) are R code, run in the R session with the data as x, so that x$mpg gives each row a bar of its mpg.

See also

heat_map, heat_map_html, heat_map_save

Author

Dillon Hammill (dillon.hammill21@gmail.com)

Examples

if(interactive() && requireNamespace("shiny", quietly = TRUE) &&
   requireNamespace("bslib", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Start with mtcars, or upload a file in the app
  heat_map_app()
  # Start from data in R, with some settings
  heat_map_app(mtcars, scale = "column", tree = "both")
}
